live.name: BRONZE SATIN
live.headline: BRONZE SATIN: what the catalogue records about this tracked threat actor
live.in_short: BRONZE SATIN is Secureworks' name for an actor also tracked as HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon. The catalogue lists two web shell tools. No report card gives more detail.

sentences.t: BRONZE SATIN is the name used in the Secureworks entry for this threat actor.
The catalogue lists three other names for the same actor: HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon.
The catalogue lists two tools for this actor: ChinaChopper and Godzilla Webshell.

next.headline: BRONZE SATIN: the espionage group also known as HAFNIUM and Silk Typhoon
next.in_short: BRONZE SATIN is Secureworks' name for a group also called HAFNIUM and Silk Typhoon. Microsoft calls it a Chinese state espionage actor. It is tied to Exchange zero-days and, more recently, IT supply chain targets.

sentences.t: Secureworks tracks this actor as BRONZE SATIN. The catalogue lists its other names as HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes Silk Typhoon as an espionage-focused Chinese state actor. It says it has tracked the group since 2020.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre judged it highly likely that HAFNIUM is associated with the Chinese state.
Microsoft says the victims of the group's recent supply chain activity were largely in state and local government and the IT sector.
BleepingComputer reports the group has hit defense contractors, policy think tanks, NGOs, healthcare, law firms and universities in the United States, Australia, Japan and Vietnam.
The catalogue lists the China Chopper and Godzilla web shells among the group's tools.
A Wikipedia article on China Chopper says Hafnium used a JScript version of it in 2021 to exploit four Microsoft Exchange zero-day flaws.
Microsoft reports that Silk Typhoon abused stolen API keys to reach the customers of IT providers. It also reports password spray attacks and zero-day exploits against edge devices.
Microsoft says the group is not known to use its own dedicated infrastructure. It typically relies on compromised covert networks, proxies and VPNs, likely to hide its operations.
In Exchange intrusions, Elastic saw web shells, credential harvesting, stolen mailbox content and new user accounts. It cautions that some of this activity may come from other opportunistic threats.
Microsoft says it began seeing Silk Typhoon exploit Exchange zero-day flaws in January 2021.
The UK government said it was almost certain that a Chinese state-backed actor started the Exchange compromise. It said over a quarter of a million servers were affected worldwide.
Microsoft, as reported by The Record, said HAFNIUM used the Log4Shell flaw to attack virtualization infrastructure.
BleepingComputer, citing a Bloomberg report, links Silk Typhoon to a December hack of the US Treasury's OFAC. Attackers reportedly used a stolen BeyondTrust API key.
In March 2025, Microsoft described a shift toward IT supply chain targets such as remote management tools, cloud applications and managed service providers.

Italian police arrested a Chinese national, Xu Zewei, on a US warrant. Italian media (ANSA) say he is accused of links to Silk Typhoon. The report calls the link an allegation, and no extradition decision is reported.
Patch internet-facing servers quickly, and treat API keys for remote management tools as sensitive credentials.
